analysis.one_liner: Lets the government negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers for Medicare's new prescription drug benefit.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2004 by the Senate's Democratic leader with no cosponsors, the bill never received a Senate vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare's prescription drug benefit was created in 2003, Congress wrote in a rule — often called the 'noninterference' clause — that specifically forbids the government from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill, sponsored by Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle, would delete that rule and instead direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices for Medicare-covered drugs, the way other big federal purchasers like the Veterans Health Administration already do. The stated goal was for Medicare beneficiaries to pay the lowest possible price for their prescriptions.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — roughly 40 million seniors and people with disabilities — would gain if the government could use Medicare's enormous buying power to negotiate lower drug prices, translating into lower out-of-pocket costs and premiums under the new Part D benefit. Taxpayers would also benefit from reduced federal drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: It deletes the 'noninterference' rule from the new Medicare drug benefit — the provision added in 2003 that barred the federal government from using Medicare's buying power to negotiate drug prices.

It directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate with drug manufacturers the way other big federal purchasers, such as the VA, already do, with the stated goal that beneficiaries 'pay the lowest possible price.'
Lower negotiated prices would flow through to seniors as lower drug costs, lower premiums, and less strain on Medicare's finances.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face downward pressure on the prices they charge for Medicare-covered drugs, and potentially bear some reduction in revenue that funds research and development. Private drug plans and middlemen in Part D could also see their role squeezed by direct negotiation.

drawbacks.text: Weakening manufacturers' pricing power could reduce the revenue that funds pharmaceutical research, potentially slowing development of new medicines — the standard objection the industry raises to government price negotiation.
The bill gave the Secretary negotiating authority but did not spell out targets, fallbacks, or deadlines, so the size and certainty of any actual savings were unproven.

The bill drew no cosponsors and was introduced months before a national election, so it was never a broadly negotiated proposal and offered no basis for the compromise that major legislation typically requires.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be large: Medicare is one of the world's biggest drug buyers, and giving it bargaining power similar to the VA's has repeatedly been estimated to save billions of dollars a year, savings that would show up as lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs for seniors and less pressure on the federal budget. The honest cost is risk to pharmaceutical innovation: manufacturers warn that government-negotiated prices — effectively the prices a buyer with no alternative can impose — would shrink the revenue that funds research into new medicines, and a hard-edged negotiating posture could lead some firms to limit which drugs they offer on Medicare terms. The bill also left design questions open — it granted authority without spelling out targets or fallbacks, which made real savings hard to guarantee. On balance it was a straightforward transfer of bargaining leverage from an industry to Medicare beneficiaries, and its death was a loss for them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee took it up, no senator cosponsored it, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill would strike the 'noninterference' section of the Medicare drug law — the provision that specifically bars the government from negotiating drug prices — and replace it with authority for the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices with manufacturers like other federal bulk buyers do.
It was introduced on July 21, 2004, read the second time two days later, and placed on the Senate Calendar under General Orders — a holding spot that carries no promise of floor time.
After that, the record shows no committee referral, no hearing, no floor debate, and no vote; the Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died on the calendar.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the legal ban on Medicare price negotiation for another fifteen-plus years, are better off that the bill died; Medicare beneficiaries kept paying prices set without government bargaining.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmaceutical makers kept the negotiation ban

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.role: Senator from South Dakota and Senate Democratic Leader (sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 21, 2004 and spoke for it in introductory remarks; it never advanced past being placed on the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, Democrat Tom Daschle, put his name on the bill, and no recorded Senate action — no hearing, debate, or vote — ever showed where the chamber stood.

industries.note: The bill's sole purpose is to remove the statutory ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices, exposing manufacturers to bulk-buying leverage comparable to the VA's. They would face downward pressure on the prices they charge the largest public drug purchaser in the country, and the industry's interest in keeping the ban ran directly against Medicare beneficiaries' interest in cheaper drugs.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plans
industries.note: The 2003 benefit routes drug purchasing through private plans and middlemen; direct government negotiation would have bypassed or squeezed part of that role. Nothing in the record shows these companies acting on the bill.
